issue.title: Dropping HTTP/2 response future doesn't cancel request body send and does not send RST_STREAM

pr.title: fix(http2): cancel pipe_task and send RST_STREAM on response future drop
pr.body:
When the client drops the response future (e.g. due to a timeout), send_task detects the cancellation but does not notify pipe_task. The pipe_task continues to hold the h2 SendStream, preventing a RST_STREAM from being sent and keeping flow-control window capacity locked.

Add a oneshot channel between send_task and pipe_task. When send_task detects cancellation via poll_canceled, it signals pipe_task through the channel. pipe_task then calls send_reset(CANCEL) on the h2 SendStream, which sends RST_STREAM to the server and frees flow-control capacity.

Closes #4040

pr.title: Fix TelegramBotHandler breaking HTML tags on split (#1990)
pr.body: Setting parseMode to HTML and hitting the length limit corrupts the message: truncation just cuts the string at a byte offset, so a `` or `` tag opened earlier in the text loses its closing tag, and Telegram's API rejects the whole message with a 400 ("can't parse entities"). Splitting has the same problem since str_split() cuts at fixed byte boundaries regardless of any tag straddling the boundary. This only changes behavior when parseMode is HTML. Truncation now backs off before any tag that got cut in half and appends closing tags for whatever is still open at the cutoff, before adding the truncated marker. Splitting tracks open tags across chunks, closes them at the end of a chunk and reopens the same tags (with their attributes, so `` survives too) at the start of the next one, shrinking the chunk further if needed to stay under the length limit. Plain text and the other parse modes still go through the original str_split()/substr() path, untouched. Added two tests in TelegramBotHandlerTest with a long `` block: one confirms truncation ends with a closed `` tag and stays under the length limit, the other confirms splitting reopens `` in every chunk and reassembles back to the original content. Ran both against the old code first to confirm they fail (unclosed/duplicated tags), then against the fix. Also ran the full TelegramBotHandlerTest suite (12 tests, 34 assertions) and phpstan on the changed file, both clean. Closes #1990

issue.title: Credentials for one proxy can be sent to a different proxy
issue.body:
During implementing of reqwest (0.13.4) into our network stack, we came across an issue with `Proxy-Authorization`. 

When more than one proxy matches a request url, `Client` chooses the proxy to connect through and the proxy to take credentials from using two separate loops that stop on different conditions.  
If a proxy without credentials is ordered ahead of one with them, the request is connected through the first proxy and sent the second's `Proxy-Authorization`. The first proxy in that case receives a basic auth that belongs to the second proxy. 


The two loops are found on `src/connect.rs:941` and `src/async_impl/client.rs:2699` (which calls `proxy.http_non_tunnel_basic_auth` to do the actual `intercept()` call).

The connect loop checks for a `Some` result on `intercept()`. This is done too in `http_non_tunnel_basic_auth()` but it ALSO returns none when there is no basic authentication found on the proxy, so two reasons for None.

issue.title: PSR-3 support
issue.body:
## Introduction

The `logError()` method of the `Slim\Handler\ErrorHandler` class currently [calls](https://github.com/slimphp/Slim/blob/2058eea946d8569323104d188814c0ba2b1d1d2d/Slim/Handlers/ErrorHandler.php#L314) the native `error_log()` function directly.

Overriding this behavior is rather tedious, as it requires:

* Subclassing `Slim\Handler\ErrorHandler` to override `logError()`
* Duplicating a lot of the [boilerplate](https://github.com/slimphp/Slim/blob/2058eea946d8569323104d188814c0ba2b1d1d2d/Slim/App.php#L154) contained in the `addErrorMiddleware()` method of `Slim\App` to manually add an instance of the `ErrorHandler` subclass

## Proposal

Modify `Slim\Handler\ErrorHandler` to receive a dependency that implements the `Psr\Log\LoggerInterface` interface from [PSR-3](https://www.php-fig.org/psr/psr-3/).

To maintain backward compatibility, make this dependency optional. If no value is specified for it, use a default implementation of the interface that implements the current behavior of calling the `error_log()` function.

Add the logger instance as a parameter of the `addErrorMiddleware()` method of `Slim\App`. Again, make this parameter optional to maintain backward compatibility.

At this point, customizing the logging behavior can be done by calling `addErrorMiddleware()` with an instance of the desired logger implementation.

## Rationale

Slim 4.x already heavily utilizes PSR standards to allow for customization including [PSR-7](https://www.php-fig.org/psr/psr-7/), [PSR-11](https://www.php-fig.org/psr/psr-11/), and [PSR-15](https://www.php-fig.org/psr/psr-15/). It also has a need for error logging, as shown in the code referenced in the previous section, and PSR-3 addresses this need.

Additionally, an attempt was made to implement PSR-3 support in Slim 3.x (see #525), so the same need has existed in at least one previous major version of Slim.

## Backward Incompatible Changes

No changes that break backward compatibility are strictly necessary to implement this change.

In a future release where backward compatibility breaks are allowed, the `$logErrors` parameter of the `__invoke()` method of `Slim\Handler\ErrorHandler` could be removed, since the logger itself could be configured to log messages or not (e.g. by using [`NullLogger`](https://github.com/php-fig/log/blob/5628725d0e4d687e29575eb41f9d5ee7de33a84c/Psr/Log/NullLogger.php)).

## Proposed Version(s)

It should be possible to include this change as suggested in Slim 4.x.

The suggestion of removing the `$logErrors` parameter could be done in Slim 5.x if desired.

## Implementation

No implementation has been created yet. However, depending on the reception of this proposal, I'd be happy to create a pull request myself.

issue.title: GzipDecompressor silently loses data from concatenated gzip members
issue.body:
### Description

I noticed that the `GzipDecompressor` class in `tornado.util` only decompresses the first gzip member when processing concatenated gzip streams, while discarding all subsequent members. Thus, this leads to data loss when handling multi member gzip files.

A gzip file can contain multiple members concatenated together, and decompressors should process all of them. This is commonly seen in HTTP responses from servers that stream gzip data and streaming applications.

### Steps to Reproduce

This is a python script to reproduce the issue:

```python
import gzip
from tornado.util import GzipDecompressor

data1 = b"This is some example data that will be compressed using gzip."
data2 = b"Here is some more example data to demonstrate gzip compression."

member1 = gzip.compress(data1)
member2 = gzip.compress(data2)
concatenated = member1 + member2

decompressor = GzipDecompressor()
decompressed_data = decompressor.decompress(concatenated)
expected_data = data1 + data2

print("Decompressed data:", decompressed_data)
print("Expected data:", expected_data)
assert decompressed_data == expected_data, "Decompressed data does not match expected data"
```

**Output:**
```
Concatenated data: b'\x1f\x8b\x08\x00\xcd\xe5:i\x02\xff\r\xc2\x81\r\x800\x08\x04\xc0U~\x02\xa7q\x01\xb4\x9f\x96\x04,\x11\x8c\xc6\xe9\xf5r\xeb\xd0\xc4?\xa7\x13|\xc4\xc3\x88&%\xa8!\x85[\xcd\xb0\x11\xfb\xf48\x99\xc9\x86+\xf5\xe8\xe8\xaf\xc6\xf2\x01c\xac%\xed=\x00\x00\x00\x1f\x8b\x08\x00\xcd\xe5:i\x02\xff\r\xc7\xc1\r\x800\x0c\x03\xc0U<\x01s\xb0FD\xad*\x12\xa9\xa3&\x0f\xc4\xf4p\xbf;\xb9\t/\x94\x82\x08\xfd\xe1c\x9171\xac\r-\x0c\x86V\xf5\xb6&\xe6\xeb\x89K\x91\x9bU\xaeu|\x90`\xd6\xcd?\x00\x00\x00'
Decompressed data:  b'This is some example data that will be compressed using gzip.'
expected data:  b'This is some example data that will be compressed using gzip.Here is some more example data to demonstrate gzip compression.'
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/home/dev/my_projects/tornado/./tornado/test/test_util.py_68-105_issue_1.py", line 22, in <module>
    assert decompressed_data == expected_data, "Decompressed data does not match expected data"
AssertionError: Decompressed data does not match expected data
```

### Expected Behavior

`GzipDecompressor` should decompress all concatenated gzip members and return the complete decompressed data.

### Actual Behavior

I observed that only the first gzip member is decompressed, while the remaining members are ignored without any note or warning, causing data loss.

### Root Cause

The implementation delegates to `zlib.decompressobj` but doesn't handle `unused_data`. When a gzip member ends, zlib places any following bytes in `.unused_data`, but `GzipDecompressor` never checks or processes this attribute, so subsequent members are lost.

### Proposed Fix

When `decompressobj.unused_data` is non-empty after decompression, it is posible to  create a new decompressor, and continue processing the unused bytes:

```python
def decompress(self, value: bytes, max_length: int = 0) -> bytes:
    if self._flushed:
        raise RuntimeError("Cannot call decompress() after flush()")

    data = value
    out = bytearray()
    remaining = max_length

    while True:
        if remaining:
            chunk = self.decompressobj.decompress(data, remaining)
        else:
            chunk = self.decompressobj.decompress(data)

        out.extend(chunk)

        if remaining:
            remaining = max(0, max_length - len(out))
            if remaining == 0:
                break

        # here it handles the concatenated gzip members:
        unused = getattr(self.decompressobj, "unused_data", b"")
        if unused:
            data = unused
            self.decompressobj = zlib.decompressobj(16 + zlib.MAX_WBITS)
            continue

        break

    return bytes(out)
```

### Test Case

The following unit test shows the issue:

```python
class TestGzipDecompressor(unittest.TestCase):
    
    def test_concatenated_gzip_members(self):
        """Testing that concatenated gzip members are fully decompressed."""
        
        data1 = b"First gzip member content."
        data2 = b"Second gzip member content."
        
        member1 = gzip.compress(data1)
        member2 = gzip.compress(data2)
        
        concatenated = member1 + member2
        decompressor = GzipDecompressor()
        result = decompressor.decompress(concatenated)
        
        
        expected = data1 + data2
        self.assertEqual(result, expected, 
                        "Concatenated gzip members should be fully decompressed")
```


### Environment

- Tornado version: tested on current master branch
- Python version: 3.12.0

pr.title: Decompress concatenated gzip members; reject trailing and truncated data
pr.body:
A gzip stream may consist of several members (RFC 1952 section 2.2). GzipDecompressor ignored everything after the first member, or, when the body was larger than chunk_size, failed with "encountered unconsumed gzip data without making progress". That error was caused by a CPython bug: when a zlib stream ends in a call that follows one cut short by max_length, the data after the end of the stream is left in unconsumed_tail as well as unused_data, and calling decompress again never consumes it. This was also the cause of the hang in #2714.

GzipDecompressor now decompresses every member, following the member loop of gzip.decompress. Each call to decompress makes one call to zlib. When a member ends, the rest of the input is read from unused_data (never the stale unconsumed_tail) and returned in unconsumed_tail, so callers that loop over unconsumed_tail pass the next member back in the same way as input that max_length held back. Data after a member must start with the gzip magic number; anything else, including NUL padding, raises zlib.error.

flush() now raises zlib.error if the stream ends partway through a member, which zlib's own flush does not detect, and raises ValueError if unconsumed_tail is not empty instead of decompressing it with no limit on the size of the output. It no longer returns any data. An empty stream (as in a response to a HEAD request) is still valid.

Calling decompress without max_length is deprecated.

_GzipMessageDelegate reports zlib errors as HTTPInputError. When finish() fails, it calls on_connection_close on the delegate it wraps, which would otherwise never hear about the message again (a client waiting on the response would hang). Its check for a call that makes no progress now also accepts a call that consumed input, since a call that finishes a member can return no output.

Fixes #3560.

issue.title: Watch mode does not rerun tests when a source file outside `root` changes and `fsModuleCache` already holds that file
issue.body:
## Describe the bug

Hi, and thank you for the work on Vitest 5.

With the default `fsModuleCache: true`, the first `vitest --watch` after a cold cache reruns a test when a linked workspace package's source (a file outside the project `root`) changes. Every later `vitest --watch` in the same checkout, once the cache holds the transformed module, prints nothing when the same file changes, and the test is not rerun. Running with `--fsModuleCache=false` restores the rerun. A file inside `root` reruns in both cases.

The failure is silent, and the cache entry persists across processes, so the same checkout behaves differently on its first and second `vitest --watch`.

Where (inferred from reading, not verified with a patch): [`transformService.ts#L324-L405`](https://github.com/vitest-dev/vitest/blob/28dc1edfb6ba5a181fe208576989063795aeadb3/packages/vitest/src/node/environments/transformService.ts#L324-L405) restores a cached module and rebuilds its `importers`/`importedModules` "to make the watch mode work" (L385), but nothing in that path registers the file with the dev server's file watcher. Vite does that while it transforms a file outside `root`, which a cache hit skips. Files inside `root` are already covered by the root watcher, which would explain why they still rerun.

## Reproduction

Repository: https://github.com/quantizor/vitest-workspace-repros/tree/main/fscache-watch (steps in the root README). The same files are inline below.

Same layout as the `@repro/lib` workspace below. There is no optimizer and no `--changed` involved.

`package.json` `{ "name": "repro-root", "private": true, "type": "module" }`, `pnpm-workspace.yaml` `packages: [ "packages/*" ]`, `.gitignore` `node_modules`.

`packages/lib/package.json`

```json
{ "name": "@repro/lib", "version": "0.0.0", "type": "module", "exports": { ".": "./src/index.ts" } }
```

`packages/lib/src/index.ts`: `export { helper } from "./helper.ts";`
`packages/lib/src/helper.ts`: `export const helper = () => 1;`

`packages/app/package.json`

```json
{
  "name": "@repro/app",
  "version": "0.0.0",
  "private": true,
  "type": "module",
  "dependencies": { "@repro/lib": "workspace:*" },
  "devDependencies": { "vitest": "5.0.4" }
}
```

`packages/app/test/uses-lib.test.ts`

```ts
import { expect, test } from "vitest";
import { helper } from "@repro/lib";

test("uses lib", () => expect(helper()).toBe(1));
```

(No `vitest.config.ts`.) Steps:

```sh
pnpm install
cd packages/app
pnpm exec vitest --watch        # first run; wait for "Waiting for file changes"
# in another terminal: edit packages/lib/src/helper.ts so it returns 2
#   -> RERUN  ../lib/src/helper.ts x1   (cold cache: works)
# stop vitest (q), then start it again:
pnpm exec vitest --watch
# edit packages/lib/src/helper.ts again
#   -> nothing is printed, no rerun (warm cache)
pnpm exec vitest --watch --fsModuleCache=false
# edit packages/lib/src/helper.ts again
#   -> RERUN  ../lib/src/helper.ts x1
```

I drove this with a script (spawn `vitest --watch`, wait for "Waiting for file changes", edit the file, wait 20 s, print what arrived). Results on 5.0.4:

```
run 1 (cold cache):       RERUN  ../lib/src/helper.ts x1     rerun triggered: true
run 2 (warm cache):       (nothing)                           rerun triggered: false
run 3 (--fsModuleCache=false):  RERUN  ../lib/src/helper.ts x1     rerun triggered: true
```

The same warm-cache run reruns for an edit to a file inside `packages/app` (`src/local.ts` imported by a test), three times out of three. A test that imports the file by a relative path (`../../lib/src/helper.ts`) behaves like the package import, so the linked symlink is not the trigger; being outside `root` is.

## Expected

Editing `packages/lib/src/helper.ts` reruns `test/uses-lib.test.ts` in watch mode, with the cache cold or warm.

## Suggested fix

On a cache hit for a file outside `root`, add the file to the environment's watcher as the uncached path does (untested).

## System Info

```shell
  System:
    OS: macOS 27.0.1
    CPU: (12) arm64 Apple M2 Pro
    Shell: 5.9 - /bin/zsh
  Binaries:
    Node: 24.11.0
    npm: 11.6.1
    pnpm: 12.8.1
  npmPackages:
    vite: 8.3.4 (transitive)
    vitest: 5.0.4 => 5.0.4
```

pnpm

issue.title: [Bug]: Timeout strategy does not propagate correct CancellationToken

pr.title: Adds caller cancellation token propagation in hedging and timeout strategies
pr.body:
# Pull Request

## The issue or feature being addressed

Fixes #3086 (Timeout strategy does not propagate the caller's `CancellationToken`)

When a resilience pipeline contains a strategy that substitutes the execution `CancellationToken` with an internal one (timeout, and also hedging), a caller-initiated cancellation surfaces an `OperationCanceledException` whose `CancellationToken` is Polly's *internal* token rather than the caller's. This breaks the common pattern of letting caller cancellation pass through unchanged while wrapping other failures, because callers cannot reliably compare `OperationCanceledException.CancellationToken` to their own token.

## Details on the issue fix or feature implementation

### Goal

Polly should throw an `OperationCanceledException` carrying the caller's token **if and only if** the cancellation was actually caused by a cancellation request on that token — for any pipeline, regardless of which strategies it is composed of or how they are nested.

### Approach

A repo-wide audit shows that within `Polly.Core` exactly two strategies substitute the execution token: **timeout** (`TimeoutResilienceStrategy`) and **hedging** (`TaskExecution` via `ResilienceContext.InitializeFrom`). Every other strategy and the pipeline plumbing only *read* `context.CancellationToken`, so they already emit the correct token at their own level.

The fix therefore lives in those two strategies, via a small shared helper:

```csharp
// Polly.Core/Utils/OutcomeUtilities.cs
public static Outcome<T> WithCallerCancellation<T>(this Outcome<T> outcome, CancellationToken callerToken)
{
    if (callerToken.IsCancellationRequested
        && outcome.Exception is OperationCanceledException oce
        && oce.CancellationToken != callerToken)
    {
        return Outcome.FromException<T>(new OperationCanceledException(callerToken).TrySetStackTrace());
    }

    return outcome;
}
```

- **Timeout** applies it to the outcome it returns, using the token that was on the context *before* it substituted its own. The existing timeout-detection branch (which produces `TimeoutRejectedException`) is unchanged.
- **Hedging** applies it at its accepted-outcome return sites, using the upstream token it already captures for the duration of the hedged execution.

Because each substituting strategy normalizes back to *its own* previous token, the behavior composes correctly through arbitrary nesting: an inner timeout rewrites to the mid-level token, the outer timeout rewrites that to the caller's token, and so on. The simplest case (`AddTimeout` only) and deeply nested cases both end up with the caller's token.

### Design decisions and trade-offs

- **Surgical fix** We considered normalizing the exception once at the outermost pipeline execution boundary. That would also cover hypothetical third-party strategies that substitute the token, but it adds work to the universal execution hot path. We chose the surgical appr

issue.title: BaseConnector: keepalive_timeout=None crashes on connection reuse (TypeError comparing float and NoneType)
issue.body:
`BaseConnector.__init__` type-hints `keepalive_timeout` as `_SENTINEL | None | float`, and only rejects `None` when `force_close=True` is also set. With the default `force_close=False`, `TCPConnector(keepalive_timeout=None)` is accepted with no error, but crashes as soon as a second request tries to reuse a pooled connection to the same host:

```
File ".../aiohttp/connector.py", line 739, in _get
    if proto.is_connected() and t1 - t0 <= self._keepalive_timeout:
TypeError: '<=' not supported between instances of 'float' and 'NoneType'
```

Repro (tested on 3.14.3 and current master):

```python
import asyncio
from aiohttp import web, ClientSession, TCPConnector

async def handler(request):
    return web.Response(text="ok")

async def main():
    app = web.Application()
    app.router.add_get("/", handler)
    runner = web.AppRunner(app)
    await runner.setup()
    site = web.TCPSite(runner, "127.0.0.1", 8765)
    await site.start()

    async with ClientSession(connector=TCPConnector(keepalive_timeout=None)) as session:
        async with session.get("http://127.0.0.1:8765/") as resp:
            print(resp.status)  # 200
        async with session.get("http://127.0.0.1:8765/") as resp:  # crashes here
            print(resp.status)

asyncio.run(main())
```

Found #786 from 2016, which looks like the same bug and got closed as fixed by #907. But #907 only handles the opposite case, it raises when `force_close=True` and `keepalive_timeout` is also set explicitly. It never touches `force_close=False` with `keepalive_timeout=None`, which is what was actually reported back then, and there's still no test for it. The `cast(float, keepalive_timeout)` in the current constructor casts away this exact `None` case for the type checker instead of handling it, probably why it's gone unnoticed this long.

Both `_get()`'s reuse check and `_cleanup()`'s deadline math need a `None` guard. Cleanup only happens to be safe right now because `weakref_handle()` silently skips scheduling when the delay is `None`, not something worth relying on.

Have a fix and regression tests ready, opening a PR shortly.

pr.title: Fix crash reusing connections when keepalive_timeout is None
pr.body:
Fixes #13756.

`BaseConnector(keepalive_timeout=None)` with the default `force_close=False` crashed on the first reused connection, since `_get()` compares idle time against `None` directly (`float <= None`). `_cleanup()` has the same bug in its deadline math, just masked because `weakref_handle()` silently skips scheduling when the delay is `None`.

Treats `None` as "never expire from idling" in both places, distinct from `force_close=True` which turns off reuse entirely, matching what the constructor's own type signature already implies.

Also dropped the `cast(float, keepalive_timeout)` on the attribute assignment, it was hiding a real mypy error for this exact case instead of handling it. There was a previous attempt at this in #907 for #786 back in 2016, but it only covered the opposite combination (`force_close=True` with an explicit `keepalive_timeout`) and never actually tested the case that got reported.

issue.title: jetstream ordered consumer uses a 15s heartbeat instead of its 5s default
issue.body:
### Observed behavior

The `jetstream` ordered consumer works out a 5s default heartbeat, but its pull subscription ends up using 15s, so a silent consumer is only noticed, and reset, after 30s instead of 10s.

`orderedConsumer.Consume` parses the options with `parseConsumeOpts(true, opts...)` ([ordered.go](https://github.com/nats-io/nats.go/blob/v1.54.0/jetstream/ordered.go#L97)), and for ordered consumers `setDefaults` picks 5s ([pull.go](https://github.com/nats-io/nats.go/blob/v1.54.0/jetstream/pull.go#L1210-L1225)). As far as I can tell, only the error handler and `StopAfter` are taken from that result though. The original `opts` go to the inner `pullConsumer.Consume` ([ordered.go](https://github.com/nats-io/nats.go/blob/v1.54.0/jetstream/ordered.go#L145)), which parses them again with `parseConsumeOpts(false, opts...)` ([pull.go](https://github.com/nats-io/nats.go/blob/v1.54.0/jetstream/pull.go#L206)) and gets the non-ordered default, `PullExpiry / 2`, which is 15s. That's the value that arms the heartbeat monitor ([pull.go](https://github.com/nats-io/nats.go/blob/v1.54.0/jetstream/pull.go#L238)) and goes into the pull requests. `Messages()` looks the same with `parseMessagesOpts` ([ordered.go](https://github.com/nats-io/nats.go/blob/v1.54.0/jetstream/ordered.go#L259), [ordered.go](https://github.com/nats-io/nats.go/blob/v1.54.0/jetstream/ordered.go#L275)). It seems to have been this way since the ordered default was added in https://github.com/nats-io/nats.go/pull/1425, and main is the same today.

I ran into it because a consumer whose inbound traffic was delayed by 25s (a toxiproxy latency toxic, with the connection staying up) never got `ErrNoHeartbeat` or reset, which I'd expected after 10s.

### Expected behavior

I'd expect an ordered consumer to use the 5s it computes, so its pull requests ask for `"idle_heartbeat":5000000000` and missing heartbeats are reported after 10s. Passing the parsed heartbeat on to the inner consumer when the user hasn't set one would probably be enough. That said, the `PullHeartbeat` docs only mention the `PullExpiry / 2` default ([jetstream_options.go](https://github.com/nats-io/nats.go/blob/v1.54.0/jetstream/jetstream_options.go#L398-L402)), so if 15s is what you actually want, the ordered branch in `setDefaults` could probably just go. Is 5s still the intended default? Happy to open a PR either way.

### Server and client version

nats.go v1.54.0 (the code is the same on main at 7685199), nats-server 2.14.7.

### Host environment

Ubuntu 24.04, nats-server in Docker, client on the host.

### Steps to reproduce

Start any `jetstream` ordered consumer with `Consume()` and watch its pull requests with the `nats` command-line tool:

```
nats sub '$JS.API.CONSUMER.MSG.NEXT.>'
```

Every request asks for a 15s heartbeat, including the one sent after the consumer is recreated. This is from the `pull-ordered` case of the reproducer in https://github.com/nats-io/nats.go/issues/2180, where `_2` is the consumer recreated after a reconnect:

```
[#1] Received on "$JS.API.CONSUMER.MSG.NEXT.KV_repro2180.w372SG8ydCLbq4eg0y18Fj_1" with reply "_INBOX.w372SG8ydCLbq4eg0y18TT"
{"expires":30000000000,"batch":500,"idle_heartbeat":15000000000}

[#2] Received on "$JS.API.CONSUMER.MSG.NEXT.KV_repro2180.w372SG8ydCLbq4eg0y18Fj_2" with reply "_INBOX.w372SG8ydCLbq4eg0y18cd"
{"expires":30000000000,"batch":500,"idle_heartbeat":15000000000}
```

pr.title: fix(jetstream): preserve ordered consumer heartbeat
pr.body:
Resolves #2181

## Root cause

`orderedConsumer.Consume` and `orderedConsumer.Messages` parse their options with `parseConsumeOpts`/`parseMessagesOpts` using `ordered=true`, which resolves the heartbeat to the ordered default of **5s** (`setDefaults` in `pull.go`). However, only `ErrHandler` and `StopAfter` were taken from that parsed result — the *original* user options were then passed to the inner `pullConsumer`, which re-parses them with `ordered=false` and therefore falls back to the generic `PullExpiry/2` default of **15s** (with the default 30s expiry).

That inner value is the one that ends up in the `idle_heartbeat` field of the pull requests and arms the heartbeat monitor, so a silent ordered consumer is only noticed and reset after ~30s instead of the intended ~10s. This has been the case since the ordered heartbeat default was introduced.

## Fix

Append the already-resolved `PullHeartbeat(consumeOpts.Heartbeat)` to the options handed to the inner consumer in both `Consume` and `Messages`:

- **Explicitly configured heartbeats are preserved**: when the user passes `jetstream.PullHeartbeat(...)`, the resolved value equals the user-provided one, so appending it is a no-op semantically.
- **Ordinary pull consumers are unaffected**: `pullConsumer.Consume`/`Messages` are unchanged; only the ordered wrappers forward the resolved value.
- Consumer resets inherit the option, since both reset paths reuse the captured option slice.

No public API, metric, or default for non-ordered consumers changes.

## Regression tests

New `TestOrderedConsumerHeartbeat` (in `jetstream/test/ordered_test.go`) subscribes to the raw `$JS.API.CONSUMER.MSG.NEXT.foo.>` subject and decodes the actual pull request payloads, asserting `idle_heartbeat` for:

1. `Consume()` with no options → expects 5s (fails before this change: 15s)
2. `Consume()` with `PullHeartbeat(10s)` → expects 10s (explicit value preserved)
3. `Consume()` with `PullExpiry(8s)` → expects 4s (expiry/2 branch of the ordered default)
4. `Messages()` with no options → expects 5s (fails before this change: 15s)
5. `Messages()` with `PullHeartbeat(10s)` → expects 10s

The two default cases were verified to fail with `idle_heartbeat=15s` on unmodified `main` (7685199) and pass with the fix.

## Validation

All run locally against nats-server 2.15.0:

- `gofmt -l` clean on changed files
- `go vet -modfile=go_test.mod ./jetstream/...` — pass
- `go test -modfile=go_test.mod -run TestOrderedConsumerHeartbeat -v ./jetstream/test/` — 5/5 pass
- `go test -modfile=go_test.mod -race -run TestOrderedConsumer ./jetstream/test/` — pass (20.4s)
- `go test -modfile=go_test.mod -run 'TestPull|TestConsume|TestMessages' ./jetstream/test/` — pass (60.6s)
- `go test -modfile=go_test.mod ./jetstream/` — pass
- `go build -modfile=go_test.mod ./...` — pass

Fixes #2181

Signed-off-by: Armin Azimi <arminazimi4030@gmail.com>

issue.title: CORS headers are missing when a middleware ends the request with an error on the Fastify adapter
issue.body:
### Is there an existing issue for this?

- [x] I have searched the existing issues

### Current behavior

Hi! 👋 On the Fastify adapter, the CORS headers of `app.enableCors()` are missing when a Nest middleware ends the request with an error:

```ts
@Injectable()
class AuthMiddleware implements NestMiddleware {
  use() {
    throw new UnauthorizedException();
  }
}

// main.ts
const app = await NestFactory.create(AppModule, new FastifyAdapter());
app.enableCors({ origin: '*' });
```

A request with an `Origin` header gets a 401 without `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`. A CORS preflight (`OPTIONS`) for the same route also runs the middleware, so it gets the 401 too, instead of a 204. The browser then shows a CORS error instead of the real 401.

On Express, the same code sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin` in the 401, and the preflight gets a 204.

I found two causes:

1. The CORS hook runs after Nest middleware. `NestFactory.create()` calls `init()` of the adapter ([`nest-factory.ts:244`](https://github.com/nestjs/nest/blob/d5d7e2c89f46b7f0f76e1d588bb092b41b4b926e/packages/core/nest-factory.ts#L244)), which registers `@fastify/middie` ([`fastify-adapter.ts:523-530`](https://github.com/nestjs/nest/blob/d5d7e2c89f46b7f0f76e1d588bb092b41b4b926e/packages/platform-fastify/adapters/fastify-adapter.ts#L523-L530)). `app.enableCors()` registers `@fastify/cors` later ([`fastify-adapter.ts:1037-1043`](https://github.com/nestjs/nest/blob/d5d7e2c89f46b7f0f76e1d588bb092b41b4b926e/packages/platform-fastify/adapters/fastify-adapter.ts#L1037-L1043)). Fastify runs `onRequest` hooks in the order of registration, so when a middleware ends the request, the CORS hook does not run.
2. A thrown error loses the headers of the Fastify reply. I registered `@fastify/cors` on the Fastify instance before `NestFactory.create()`, so that its hook runs first. The preflight then works, but a middleware that throws, or that returns a rejected promise, still gives a 401 without the header. `RouterProxy` catches that error ([`router-proxy.ts:20-25`](https://github.com/nestjs/nest/blob/d5d7e2c89f46b7f0f76e1d588bb092b41b4b926e/packages/core/router/router-proxy.ts#L20-L25)), and the exception filter answers on the raw Node.js response. For a raw response, `FastifyAdapter.reply()` makes a new, empty `Reply` ([`fastify-adapter.ts:694-708`](https://github.com/nestjs/nest/blob/d5d7e2c89f46b7f0f76e1d588bb092b41b4b926e/packages/platform-fastify/adapters/fastify-adapter.ts#L694-L708)), so the headers set earlier with `reply.header()` are not sent. A middleware that passes the same error to `next()` keeps the header, because the Fastify error handler still has the original reply.

The `cors` option of `NestFactory.create()` has the same order problem. It also calls `enableCors()`, from `app.init()` ([`nest-application.ts:199`](https://github.com/nestjs/nest/blob/d5d7e2c89f46b7f0f76e1d588bb092b41b4b926e/packages/core/nest-application.ts#L199)), so it is registered after middie too. I tested it with `cors: { origin: '*' }`, and it gives the same results as `app.enableCors()`.

The built-in security headers do not have these problems. Their hook is added in the constructor, before middie, and it sets the headers on `reply.raw` ([`fastify-adapter.ts:409-423`](https://github.com/nestjs/nest/blob/d5d7e2c89f46b7f0f76e1d588bb092b41b4b926e/packages/platform-fastify/adapters/fastify-adapter.ts#L409-L423)).

I am not sure what the best fix is, so I would like to ask first 🙂 One option for the order is to add the CORS hook before middie, like the security hook. One option for the lost headers is to let `reply()` keep the headers of the original Fastify reply when it gets a raw response. I am happy to open a PR for the option that you prefer. Today, a workaround is to register `@fastify/cors` before `NestFactory.create()` and to call `next(err)` in the middleware instead of `throw`.

### Minimum reproduction code

https://github.com/johnnyhuirilef/nestjs-repros/tree/main/fastify-cors-middleware-error

### Steps to reproduce

```bash
git clone https://github.com/johnnyhuirilef/nestjs-repros
cd nestjs-repros/fastify-cors-middleware-error
npm install
npm run repro
```

The script runs three setups: Express with `enableCors()`, Fastify with `enableCors()`, and Fastify with `@fastify/cors` registered before `NestFactory.create()`. Each setup gets four requests: `GET /ok` (no middleware), `GET /throw` (the middleware throws), `GET /next-error` (the middleware calls `next(err)`) and `OPTIONS /throw` (a preflight). All four Express responses send `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`. The Fastify responses that do not match Express:

```
=== fastify (enableCors): GET /throw ===
  status:                      HTTP 401
  access-control-allow-origin: undefined
  expected:                    HTTP 401, "*"

=== fastify (enableCors): GET /next-error ===
  status:                      HTTP 401
  access-control-allow-origin: undefined
  expected:                    HTTP 401, "*"

=== fastify (enableCors): OPTIONS /throw ===
  status:                      HTTP 401
  access-control-allow-origin: undefined
  expected:                    HTTP 204, "*"

=== fastify (cors before middleware): GET /throw ===
  status:                      HTTP 401
  access-control-allow-origin: undefined
  expected:                    HTTP 401, "*"

RESULT: BUG: 4 of 12 responses do not match Express.
```

The README of the repro has the full output.

### Expected behavior

The Fastify adapter answers like the Express adapter: the error response of a middleware has the CORS headers, and the preflight gets a 204 with the CORS headers.

### NestJS version

12.2.0

### Packages versions

```
@nestjs/common: 12.2.0
@nestjs/core: 12.2.0
@nestjs/platform-express: 12.2.0
@nestjs/platform-fastify: 12.2.0
fastify: 5.12.7
@fastify/cors: 11.3.1
```

### Node.js version

24.21.0

### In which operating systems have you tested?

- [x] macOS
- [ ] Windows
- [ ] Linux

### Other

`packages/platform-fastify` and `packages/core/router` on master (d5d7e2c89) have no changes since v12.2.0.

A similar report, #9510, was closed in 2022 as a support question. This issue adds the two causes in the adapter and a repro on 12.2.0.

pr.title: fix(fastify): run cors before nest middleware
pr.body:
## What is the current behavior?

On Fastify, `app.enableCors()` (and the `cors` option) registers `@fastify/cors` after `NestFactory.create()` has already registered middie. Its `onRequest` hook therefore runs after Nest middleware. This has two effects:

- A preflight request goes through the middleware, so an auth middleware rejects it.
- A response that a middleware ends, or fails with, has no CORS headers.

On Express, `cors` runs before Nest middleware.

Closes #18212

## What is the new behavior?

- The adapter adds a delegating `onRequest` hook in its constructor, like the 503 and security hooks. The hook sits after the 503 hook and before the security hook, so CSRF and security-header responses also carry the CORS headers.
- `enableCors()` registers `@fastify/cors` on the root context and keeps the request hook the plugin adds, so the constructor's hook runs it. The plugin's other calls (`decorateRequest`, the `OPTIONS *` route) go to the instance as before.
- After the CORS hook runs, its `vary` and `access-control-*` headers are copied to the Node.js response. Without this, a response a middleware ends itself, or the error response of a middleware that throws, would not carry them. That error response is sent through a new reply. When Fastify sends the reply itself, the reply's own header values still win.
- A `hook` option other than `onRequest` (e.g. `preHandler`) is registered exactly as before; it runs after middleware either way.
- A function passed as the options is handled two ways:
  - One that takes the instance is still called for the options, as `register()` does.
  - An options delegate taking `(request, callback)`, the shape of the `cors` option's `CorsOptionsDelegate`, is now passed to `@fastify/cors` as its delegate. Before, `register()` called it with the instance and startup failed.

Trade-offs worth a look:

- CORS now runs before Nest middleware and before user `onRequest` hooks, so preflights no longer reach them. This matches Express.
- Removing a CORS header in a handler with `reply.removeHeader()` no longer removes it from the response, because it was also set on the raw response.

## Tests

The new `integration/cors/e2e/middleware.spec.ts` uses both Express and Fastify via `NestFactory.create()`, covering `enableCors()`, the `cors` option, an options delegate and, on Fastify, an options factory. It checks four things:

- a middleware's 401 carries `Access-Control-Allow-Origin`;
- a response the middleware ends itself carries it;
- the preflight is answered with 204 and the middleware is not run;
- the handler's response carries it.

A last case checks `hook: 'preHandler'`.

On master, the Fastify cases fail: the error and ended responses lack the header, and the delegate setup fails to start. Without the raw-header copy, the error and ended cases fail.

## Does this PR introduce a breaking change?

- [ ] Yes
- [x] No (but see the trade-offs above)

issue.title: dns interceptor: fetch fails with ERR_ASSERTION when the response is preceded by 103 Early Hints
issue.body:
## Bug Description

When I compose `interceptors.dns()` into an `Agent`, any response that is preceded by an interim `1xx` response (in my case `103 Early Hints`) fails with `TypeError: fetch failed`. The cause is an `AssertionError` from `DecoratorHandler.onResponseStart`:

```
assert(!this.#onResponseStartCalled)
```

Both the HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 clients deliver interim responses through `onResponseStart` before the final one, so the final `200` is the second `onResponseStart` call on `DNSDispatchHandler` (which extends `DecoratorHandler`) and trips the once-only assertion.

I hit this in production fetching Cloudflare-hosted pages (for example usafacts.org and Substack posts): Cloudflare sends `103 Early Hints` over HTTP/2, and every such page failed through my DNS-pinning dispatcher. The same requests without the dns interceptor succeed.

## Reproduction

**Standalone reproduction script:**

```javascript
'use strict'

const { test } = require('node:test')
const { createServer } = require('node:http')
const { once } = require('node:events')
const { Agent, fetch, interceptors } = require('undici')

async function earlyHintsServer (t) {
  const server = createServer((req, res) => {
    res.writeEarlyHints({ link: '</style.css>; rel=preload; as=style' })
    res.writeHead(200, { 'content-type': 'text/plain' })
    res.end('ok')
  })
  t.after(() => { server.closeAllConnections?.(); server.close() })
  server.listen(0)
  await once(server, 'listening')
  return `http://localhost:${server.address().port}/`
}

test('103 Early Hints without the dns interceptor', { timeout: 60000 }, async (t) => {
  t.plan(1)
  const url = await earlyHintsServer(t)
  const dispatcher = new Agent()
  t.after(() => dispatcher.close())

  const res = await fetch(url, { dispatcher })
  t.assert.strictEqual(await res.text(), 'ok')
})

test('103 Early Hints with the dns interceptor', { timeout: 60000 }, async (t) => {
  t.plan(1)
  const url = await earlyHintsServer(t)
  const dispatcher = new Agent().compose(interceptors.dns())
  t.after(() => dispatcher.close())

  const res = await fetch(url, { dispatcher })
  t.assert.strictEqual(await res.text(), 'ok')
})
```

On undici 8.12.2 the first test passes and the second fails.

Versions I tested:

| undici | HTTP/1.1 + 103 | HTTP/2 + 103 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 7.29.1 | fails | not tested |
| 8.9.0 | fails | works |
| 8.10.0 | fails | works |
| 8.10.1 | fails | fails |
| 8.11.2 | fails | fails |
| 8.12.2 | fails | fails |

For HTTP/2 I used a `node:http2` `createSecureServer` that calls `stream.additionalHeaders({ ':status': 103, link: '...' })` before `stream.respond({ ':status': 200 })`, fetched with `new Agent({ allowH2: true, connect: { rejectUnauthorized: false } }).compose(interceptors.dns())`. It works in 8.10.0 and fails from 8.10.1, which is the release containing #5712 (forwarding 1xx responses on HTTP/2). A plain `Agent` works on both protocols in every version above.

## Expected Behavior

Interim `1xx` responses don't count as the response start, and the request resolves with the final `200` and body `ok`. `fetch` itself already ignores `status < 200` in its `onResponseStart`.

## Actual Behavior

`fetch` rejects with `TypeError: fetch failed` whose `cause` is `AssertionError [ERR_ASSERTION]`.

## Logs & Screenshots

```
TypeError: fetch failed
  [cause]: AssertionError [ERR_ASSERTION]: The expression evaluated to a falsy value:

    assert(!this.#onResponseStartCalled)

      at DNSDispatchHandler.onResponseStart (undici/lib/handler/decorator-handler.js:35:5)
      at Request.onResponseStart (undici/lib/core/request.js:345:39)
      at ClientHttp2Stream.onResponse (undici/lib/dispatcher/client-h2.js:1449:15)
```

## Environment

- OS: Ubuntu, Linux 6.8.0
- Node.js version: v24.19.0
- undici version: 8.12.2 (also 7.29.1 through 8.11.2, see the table above)

### Additional context

A fix might be for `DecoratorHandler.onResponseStart` to skip the once-only check (and not set the flag) when `statusCode < 200`. As a workaround I compose an innermost interceptor that drops `onResponseStart` calls with `statusCode < 200` before they reach the dns interceptor's handler.

## Rationale

The HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 clients deliver interim `1xx` responses (e.g. `103 Early Hints`) through `onResponseStart` before the final response. `DecoratorHandler.onResponseStart` asserts it is only called once, so any handler built on it (the dns interceptor's `DNSDispatchHandler` in the issue) fails the request with `ERR_ASSERTION` when the final response arrives after an interim one.

## Changes

- `DecoratorHandler.onResponseStart` only applies the once-only check (and sets the flag) for final responses (`statusCode >= 200`). Interim responses are still forwarded to the wrapped handler, which already ignores them where needed (e.g. `fetch`).
- Tests: a `DecoratorHandler` unit test (a `103` then a `200` are both forwarded, and a second final response still asserts), and a dns interceptor test fetching from a server that sends `103 Early Hints`. Both fail on `main`.

issue.title: hyperfine panics on broken pipe (EPIPE) for all run-output paths
issue.body:
## Bug description

Hyperfine panics when its standard output stream is closed while benchmark results are being printed — e.g. when piping to a program that exits early:

```
$ hyperfine --runs 1 "echo hi" | head -n 0
thread 'main' (1234) panicked at library/std/src/io/stdio.rs:1166:9:
failed printing to stdout: Broken pipe (os error 32)
note: run with `RUST_BACKTRACE=1` environment variable to display a backtrace
```

(exit code 101)

This affects every code path that prints results to stdout:

* the `Benchmark N: …` header and `Time`/`Range` result lines (`src/benchmark/mod.rs`)
* the `Summary` / `Relative speed comparison` tables (`src/benchmark/scheduler.rs`)
* export to stdout via `--export-json -`, `--export-markdown -`, etc. (`src/export/mod.rs`, `ExportTarget::Stdout`)

This is the same bug class as #453, which was closed by fixing only the `-h`/`--help` output (handled inside clap). All `println!` sites reachable during an actual benchmark run still panic on `EPIPE` (Unix) / `ERROR_BROKEN_PIPE` (Windows).

Unix command-line tools conventionally terminate quietly when their output pipe is closed (they die from `SIGPIPE`). Rust ignores `SIGPIPE`, so the write error surfaces as a panic in `println!` instead.

## Expected behavior

`hyperfine … | head -n 0` should terminate quietly without a panic message, the same as other CLI tools.

## Steps to reproduce

On Unix, `hyperfine --runs 1 "echo hi" | head -n 0` usually reproduces it (timing-dependent). Deterministic version, with the pipe's read end closed before spawn:

```python
import os, subprocess
r, w = os.pipe()
os.close(r)
p = subprocess.Popen(["hyperfine", "--runs", "1", "echo hi"], stdout=w)
os.close(w)
p.wait()
print(p.returncode)  # 101, with the panic message on stderr
```

The same panic occurs for `hyperfine --runs 1 --export-json - "echo hi"`, `--export-markdown -`, and for multiple commands (summary table). On Windows it was verified as `hyperfine --runs 1 "cmd /c echo hi" | exit0.exe` where `exit0.exe` exits immediately (panic with `os error 232`, `ERROR_BROKEN_PIPE`).

## Suggested fix

Replace the `println!` calls that write to stdout with `writeln!(io::stdout(), …)` and propagate the `io::Error` (the surrounding functions already return `Result` or can return `Result`); then, in `main()`, treat `io::ErrorKind::BrokenPipe` as a quiet `exit(0)` — matching how e.g. Cargo and other CLI tools handle a closed output stream. A candidate patch implementing this, including a regression test that runs hyperfine with a pre-closed stdout pipe, is available on my fork (`fix/broken-pipe` branch, https://github.com/Mathjk/hyperfine/tree/fix/broken-pipe). It also converts the `eprintln!` warning paths to error-propagating `writeln!` calls so a closed stderr is handled the same way.

## Version

hyperfine 1.20.0 (master @ f12f3d9)

---
*This issue report was prepared with AI assistance; the bug itself was verified by reproduction on Linux and Windows.*

```markdown

   field is `b"a"` and computes a valid HMAC using the configured secret:

   from tornado.web import _create_signature_v2, decode_signed_value

   def field(value: bytes) -> bytes:

pr.body:
Fixes #3701

`decode_signed_value` raises `ValueError` when a v1 or v2 signed value has a syntactically malformed (non-decimal) timestamp, even after the HMAC signature has verified. `RequestHandler.get_signed_cookie` documents that invalid signed values return `None`, so this path should reject rather than raise into request handling.

This is not a signature bypass: producing such an input requires the signing key. A malformed value from a key-holding component (or during key rotation) can still turn into an unhandled exception instead of a clean rejection.

Wrap the `int()` conversion in both `_decode_signed_value_v1` and `_decode_signed_value_v2` and return `None` on `ValueError`, consistent with the other rejection paths in those functions.

Added `test_malformed_timestamp_v1` and `test_malformed_timestamp_v2`, which build correctly signed values with non-decimal timestamps and assert they decode to `None`. The full `SignedValueTest` suite passes (12 tests).

issue.title: fix($subscribe): duplicate watcher fires callback twice on direct mutations when same callback subscribed twice
issue.body:
When the same callback reference is passed to `$subscribe` more than once, `$patch` correctly calls it only once (the subscriptions Set deduplicates), but **direct state mutations** (`store.prop = value`) call it **once per subscription** because each call unconditionally creates a new Vue watcher that fires independently.

### Reproduction

```ts
import { setActivePinia, createPinia, defineStore } from "pinia"

setActivePinia(createPinia())

const useStore = defineStore("main", {
  state: () => ({ user: "Eduardo" }),
})
const store = useStore()

let callCount = 0
const callback = () => { callCount++ }

store.$subscribe(callback, { flush: "sync" })
store.$subscribe(callback, { flush: "sync" }) // same reference

// Direct mutation: triggers one watcher per subscribe call
store.$state.user = "Cleiton"
console.log(callCount) // Expected: 1, Actual: 2  ← BUG

// $patch: uses triggerSubscriptions(Set), correctly fires once
store.$patch({ user: "Other" })
console.log(callCount) // Expected: 2, Actual: 3  ← BUG (2 from watcher, 1 from patch)
```

### Root cause

PR #2887 changed the internal `subscriptions` collection from an `Array` to a `Set` to prevent duplicates. `Set.add` is idempotent so `triggerSubscriptions` (used by `$patch`) calls the callback only once. However, `$subscribe` still creates a new `watch()` call on **every invocation**, regardless of whether the callback is already in the Set. N duplicate subscriptions therefore produce N watchers that each independently invoke the callback on direct state mutations.

### Expected behavior

If the same callback reference is already subscribed, `$subscribe` should be idempotent — consistent with the Set semantics already used for `$patch`.

### Additional context

- Introduced by #2887 ("refactor: change Subscription Array to Subscription Set")
- Both options-store and setup-store variants are affected
- `$onAction` is not affected (it does not create a watcher)

But `$subscribe` unconditionally created a new Vue `watch()` on every call, causing each watcher to fire the callback independently on direct state mutations (`store.prop = value`). issue.title: --opt= silently collapses to a bare flag and consumes the following token (short -o= behaves differently)
issue.body:
## Description

`ParsedArgument.init(_:)` (`Sources/ArgumentParser/Parsing/SplitArguments.swift`, ~lines 21–31) collapses an empty value after `=` into a bare flag:

```swift
let indexOfEqualSign = str.firstIndex(of: "=") ?? str.endIndex
let (baseName, value) = (str[..<indexOfEqualSign], str[indexOfEqualSign...].dropFirst())
let name = Name(baseName)
self = value.isEmpty ? .name(name) : .nameWithValue(name, String(value))
```

Double-dash tokens reach this initializer whole, so `--out=` becomes `.name(.long("out"))`. A value-taking `@Option` then consumes the **next** token via `popNextElementIfValue(after:)`, meaning:

```
prog --out= file.txt
```

parses as `out = "file.txt"` — the user's positional/file argument is silently swallowed as the option value, with no diagnostic. Every downstream positional shifts.

The single-dash path (`SplitArguments.swift` ~743–750) behaves differently and correctly: `-o=` produces `.nameWithValue(.short("o"), "")`, preserving the explicit empty string and leaving `file.txt` positional. Identical user intent (`--opt=` is GNU-conventional for an empty-string value), divergent silent outcomes.

Static trace through `parseIndividualArg` → `Name` dash-stripping → option value-pop against today's main; no Swift toolchain locally, so not executed.

## Steps to Reproduce

```swift
struct O: ParsableArguments {
    @Option(name: .long) var out: String
    @Argument var file: String
}
// input: ["--out=", "file.txt"]
// current: out="file.txt", missing positional → or silently misassigned
```

## Expected Behavior

`--out=` should yield `nameWithValue(.long("out"), "")` exactly like `-o=` does for short flags: the user explicitly typed a value slot, so the empty string is intentional and the following token must remain positional.

## Actual Behavior

Empty value collapses to a bare flag; the next token is consumed as the value.

## Impact

Silent misassignment of user data to the wrong parameter — worst case an input file path becomes an option value. No error surfaces; parsing succeeds with shifted semantics.

## Suggested Direction

Treat presence of `=` as authoritative regardless of value emptiness for long options:

```swift
self = str.contains("=") || !value.isEmpty
    ? .nameWithValue(name, String(value))
    : .name(name)
```

(keeping short-option behavior unchanged), plus regression tests for `["--out=", "file.txt"]` vs `["-o=", "file.txt"]`.

pr.title: Fix --opt= silently consuming the next positional token
pr.body:
### Motivation

Fixes #958.

`ParsedArgument.init(_:)` treated a long option with an empty value after `=` (e.g. `--out=`) identically to a bare long option (e.g. `--out`). The initializer would collapse `--out=` to `.name(.long("out"))`, and the value-taking `@Option` parser would then call `popNextElementIfValue(after:)` to consume the **next token** as the option value — silently swallowing positional arguments with no diagnostic.

Short options did not have this bug: `-o=` already produced `.nameWithValue(.short("o"), "")`.

### Modifications

**`Sources/ArgumentParser/Parsing/SplitArguments.swift`**

Track whether `=` was present in the raw input independently of whether the value substring is empty:

```swift
// Before
self = value.isEmpty ? .name(name) : .nameWithValue(name, String(value))

// After
let hasEqualSign = indexOfEqualSign != str.endIndex
self = hasEqualSign || !value.isEmpty
    ? .nameWithValue(name, String(value))
    : .name(name)
```

When `=` is present, `--out=` now produces `.nameWithValue(.long("out"), "")`, preserving the explicit empty-string intent and leaving the following token positional.

**Tests**

- `Tests/ArgumentParserUnitTests/SplitArgumentTests.swift` — four unit tests:
  - `longOptionWithEmptyValue`: `--out=` → `.nameWithValue(.long("out"), "")`
  - `shortOptionWithEmptyValue`: `-o=` → `.nameWithValue(.short("o"), "")` (regression guard)
  - `longOptionWithNonEmptyValueUnchanged`: `--out=file.txt` unchanged
  - `longOptionWithoutEqualsSign`: `--out` still produces bare `.name`

- `Tests/ArgumentParserEndToEndTests/EqualsEndToEndTests.swift` — four end-to-end tests confirming that `["--out=", "file.txt"]` parses as `out="", file="file.txt"` rather than `out="file.txt"` with a missing positional.

All 264 tests pass (260 pre-existing + 4 new).

pr.title: feat(http1): add max_header_size limit for server and client
pr.body:
## Motivation
Resolves #3832.

Currently, HTTP/1 header size limits can only be indirectly bounded using `max_buf_size`. However, setting `max_buf_size` also restricts the maximum single read buffer for streaming request or response bodies. Furthermore, there was an existing TODO in `proto/h1/conn.rs` noting that `h1_max_header_size` should be wired up to the chunked decoder for trailers.

This PR adds explicit `max_header_size(bytes)` configuration options to both `server::conn::http1::Builder` and `client::conn::http1::Builder`.

## Solution & Architecture
- **Server Builder (`server::conn::http1::Builder`)**:
  - Exposes `pub fn max_header_size(&mut self, val: usize) -> &mut Self`.
  - Configures the maximum total size of HTTP/1 request headers (request line + headers) in bytes.
  - When exceeded, the server responds with `431 Request Header Fields Too Large` (RFC 6585 §5) and closes the connection.
- **Client Builder (`client::conn::http1::Builder`)**:
  - Exposes `pub fn max_header_size(&mut self, val: usize) -> &mut Self`.
  - Configures the maximum total size of HTTP/1 response headers (status line + headers) in bytes.
  - When exceeded, the client returns an error where `error.is_parse_too_large() == true`.
- **Early Enforcement**:
  - Enforced in `io::Buffered::parse_headers` as bytes are read, preventing buffering unbounded amounts of header data.
  - Enforced in `Server::parse` / `Client::parse` against `parsed_len` to protect scenarios where a single read buffer already contains subsequent data.
- **Chunked Trailers**:
  - Replaced the pre-existing `// TODO: remove this when we land h1_max_header_size support` placeholder in `proto::h1::conn.rs` (`decode::Decoder::new`) with the configured `h1_max_header_size`.

## Verification
- Unit test in `src/proto/h1/role.rs`:
  - `test_h1_max_header_size`: Tests exact boundary conditions on both server and client parsers.
- Integration tests in `tests/server.rs`:
  - `max_header_size_exceeded`: Verifies server returns `431 Request Header Fields Too Large` when request header size exceeds limit.
  - `max_header_size_accepted`: Verifies server accepts requests when within limit.
  - `max_header_size_with_large_max_buf_size`: Verifies `max_header_size` enforcement is decoupled from and strictly enforced even when `max_buf_size` is large.
- Integration tests in `tests/client.rs`:
  - `client_max_header_size_exceeded`: Verifies client errors with `is_parse_too_large() == true`.
  - `client_max_header_size_accepted`: Verifies client successfully receives responses within limit.
- All test suites passing (`cargo test --lib --features full`, `cargo test --test server --features full`, `cargo test --test client --features full`).

## Summary

- Fixes #1996 — the per-target `level` filter was silently ignored when `pino.transport({ targets: [...] })` contained a single element.

pr.title: Add continue_callback to answer Expect: 100-continue before the body is read
pr.body:
### Description

Closes #3188.

Puma replies `100 Continue` to every request that sends `Expect: 100-continue`, so an app can't turn a request away before the client uploads the body — redirecting an upload elsewhere or refusing an oversized one means receiving it all first. `Client#setup_body` has carried `# TODO allow a hook here to check the headers before going forward` for this.

This implements the shape @nateberkopec proposed and @dentarg agreed in the issue, with `false` as the no-op per @dentarg's suggestion:

```ruby
continue_callback do |env|
  env['CONTENT_LENGTH'].to_i > 10_000_000 ? [413, {}, []] : false
end
```

- **`false` / `nil`** — unchanged behaviour: `100 Continue` is sent and the request reaches the app.
- **A Rack response** — sent instead. `100 Continue` is not sent, the body is never read, the app is not called, and the connection is closed.

Without the option, nothing changes.

**Decisions worth checking**

- **It reuses the existing pre-body rejection path.** `http_content_length_limit` already refuses a request before reading its body, by raising from `setup_body` and letting `client_error` write the response. This does the same with a new `ContinueRejected` that carries the callback's response, so it's answered correctly whether `setup_body` ran on the reactor or in the thread pool — both already rescue into `client_error` and then close the client. That's also why it adds no logging: answering early is the callback working, not an error.
- **The connection is always closed after a rejection.** The client may already have started sending the body (curl does after a short wait), and Puma won't read it, so the connection can't safely be reused. This mirrors what the 413 path does.
- **The callback can run on the reactor thread**, which services every connection still waiting for its request, so a slow callback would stall them. The DSL docs say to decide from the headers alone and not do I/O in it. If you'd rather Puma enforce something here, I'm happy to change it.
- **I didn't validate the returned status.** The docs say 3xx or 4xx; returning anything else is the app's choice. I can add a guard if you'd prefer one.

This supersedes #3200, which was closed as stale in November 2024.

pr.title: Don't send content-length: 0 for 304 responses with an empty body
pr.body:
### Description
When a Rack app returns a 304 with an empty body and no `content-length` header, Puma calculates the length from the body and sends `content-length: 0`. RFC 9110 §8.6 says a server must not send Content-Length in a 304 unless it equals the size the 200 response would have had, and Puma has no way to know that size.

This change extends the existing 204 handling from #2896 to 304. Puma no longer calculates the length for 304, so it never sends a value it made up. A `content-length` header the app sets itself still passes through, because the RFC allows that.

I didn't use `STATUS_WITH_NO_ENTITY_BODY` because it also includes 205. For 205, sending `content-length: 0` is the recommended behavior (RFC 9110 §15.3.6), so using it would change 205 responses too.

Follows the review on #3993 (scope to 304).

pr.body:

issue.title: MSSQL: lock table hint emitted outside nested join parentheses, producing invalid SQL (1.1.0 regression)
issue.body:
### Issue description

mssql + TypeORM 1.1.0: a lock combined with a two-level relation join emits WITH (NOLOCK) outside the nested join's parentheses, so the query fails with Incorrect syntax near the keyword 'with'. 1.1.0 regression.

### Expected Behavior

A query with a relation chain of depth >= 2 and `setLock()` should produce valid T-SQL,
with the table hint attached to each table reference.

### Actual Behavior

The hint is appended after the closing `)` of the nested join, where a table hint is not
allowed, and the inner table loses its hint entirely. SQL Server fails with:

```
QueryFailedError: Error: Incorrect syntax near the keyword 'with'. If this statement is a
common table expression, an xmlnamespaces clause or a change tracking context clause, the
previous statement must be terminated with a semicolon.
```

### Steps to reproduce

Entities (three distinct entities, plain many-to-one — nothing special about them):

```ts
@Entity() class Country { @PrimaryColumn() id: number }

@Entity() class Profile {
  @PrimaryColumn() id: number
  @Column() countryId: number
  @ManyToOne(() => Country) @JoinColumn({ name: 'countryId' }) country: Country
}

@Entity() class User {
  @PrimaryColumn() id: number
  @Column() profileId: number
  @ManyToOne(() => Profile) @JoinColumn({ name: 'profileId' }) profile: Profile
}
```

Depth 1 — **valid**:

```ts
repo.createQueryBuilder('u').leftJoinAndSelect('u.profile', 'p').setLock('dirty_read')
```
```sql
FROM "user" "u" WITH (NOLOCK) LEFT JOIN "profile" "p" WITH (NOLOCK) ON "p"."id"="u"."profileId"
```

Depth 2 — **invalid**:

```ts
repo.createQueryBuilder('u')
  .leftJoinAndSelect('u.profile', 'p')
  .leftJoinAndSelect('p.country', 'c')
  .setLock('dirty_read')
```
```sql
FROM "user" "u" WITH (NOLOCK) LEFT JOIN ("profile" "p" LEFT JOIN "country" "c" WITH (NOLOCK) ON "c"."id"="p"."countryId") WITH (NOLOCK) ON "p"."id"="u"."profileId"
--                            ^ hint missing on "p"                                                                    ^ hint illegal here
```

Also reproduces through find options, so it is not query-builder specific:

```ts
repo.find({ relations: { profile: { country: true } }, lock: { mode: 'dirty_read' } })
```

And with the other two lock modes — `pessimistic_read` → `WITH (HOLDLOCK, ROWLOCK)`,
`pessimistic_write` → `WITH (UPDLOCK, ROWLOCK)` — in the same wrong position.

Depth 2 *without* a lock is valid, so the parenthesised nesting itself is fine; only the
hint placement is wrong.


### My Environment

| Dependency | Version |
| --- | --- |
| operating system | Linux |
| typeorm | 1.1.0 (works on 1.0.0 and 0.3.29) |
| driver | mssql |


### Additional Context

Regression appeared between 1.0.0 and 1.1.0: on 1.0.0 and 0.3.29 the same code emits every
join flat, with no parentheses, so the hint is always attached to a table reference.

pr.title: fix(mssql): place table lock hint inside nested join parentheses
pr.body:
Fixes #12764

### Description of change

On SQL Server, a relation chain two levels deep combined with `setLock()` produced invalid T-SQL. The table hint landed after the closing parenthesis of the nested join, where SQL Server does not allow one, and the inner table was left without a hint at all:

```sql
LEFT JOIN ("profile" "p" LEFT JOIN "country" "c" WITH (NOLOCK) ON ...) WITH (NOLOCK) ON ...
```

The query then failed with `Incorrect syntax near the keyword 'with'`. Nesting the joins in parentheses came in with #11137, but `buildJoinClause` still appended the hint after `postfix`, so once a join had children the hint drifted outside the parentheses instead of staying on its own table reference. Moving the call in front of `childJoins` puts the hint straight after the alias it belongs to, which is where the flat (depth 1) case already put it:

```sql
LEFT JOIN ("profile" "p" WITH (NOLOCK) LEFT JOIN "country" "c" WITH (NOLOCK) ON ...) ON ...
```

Verified with a new test in `test/functional/query-builder/locking`, which fails on `master` and passes here. The full suite runs green against SQL Server 2025.

issue.title: Expose Flag.SchemaType() for typed flag introspection
issue.body:
## Summary

Expose typed-schema introspection on `cli.Flag`:

```go
// SchemaType returns the JSON Schema type name for the value this flag
// accepts: "boolean", "integer", "number", "string", "array".
// Returns "" if the flag does not map cleanly to a JSON Schema type.
//
// For slice flags, the returned type is "array"; callers can use
// SchemaItemsType for the element type.
func (f Flag) SchemaType() string
func (f Flag) SchemaItemsType() string // optional, for slice flags
```

## Motivation

[cli-mcp](https://github.com/coilysiren/cli-mcp) projects a urfave/cli command tree as a Model Context Protocol server. MCP tools carry a JSON Schema for their input, derived from the command's flags. Today this is a mechanical type-switch:

```go
switch f.(type) {
case *cli.BoolFlag:
    s.Type = "boolean"
case *cli.IntFlag, *cli.Int8Flag, *cli.Int16Flag, *cli.Int32Flag, *cli.Int64Flag:
    s.Type = "integer"
case *cli.UintFlag, *cli.Uint8Flag, ... :
    s.Type = "integer"
case *cli.FloatFlag:
    s.Type = "number"
case *cli.StringSliceFlag:
    s.Type = "array"  // items: string
case *cli.IntSliceFlag:
    s.Type = "array"  // items: integer
// ... etc
}
```

This is brittle - every new flag type urfave ships (or that consumers add via the third-party flag system) requires a code change in every extension. A `SchemaType()` method on Flag (or a `Type` constant) would let extensions stop pattern-matching on concrete types.

This same need exists for:

- **cli-web-ops** — rendering JSON Schema input as HTML form fields (`<input type="text|number|checkbox">`)
- **cli-web-docs** — rendering flag types in generated documentation
- **urfave/cli-docs** itself — currently maps flag types in Markdown output by similar type switching

## Alternatives considered

- A standalone `cli-schema-types` helper. Forces a hard-coded import dependency just for type strings.
- Reflection. Works but is fragile and slow.

The right home is the Flag interface itself, since the flag knows its own type.

Happy to send a PR if there's appetite. Could plausibly be hidden behind a feature flag or new `DocFlag` interface to preserve backwards compatibility with third-party flag types.

issue.title: Deprecate unneeded `ETagSet` methods
issue.body:
`contains` and `contains_weak` are the only correct methods, and match the strong and weak comparisons described in RFC 9110. None of the other methods are used by the code or required by any spec.

- `is_weak` is incorrect, it only checks if the value is in the weak set, but that's not the weak comparison function.
- `is_strong` is incorrect, it only checks if the value is in the strong set, but skips the star check.
- `contains_raw` decides what `contains` method to use based on if the parsed ETag is marked weak. But that's incorrect, which comparison to use is based on the header being evaluated, not the incoming ETag.
- `__call__` kind of fixes the problem with `contains_raw` by allowing to choose which comparison method to use with a parameter. But it also allows passing `data` to call `generate_etag`, which is not used anywhere and can be done as `contains(generate_etag(data))`.
- `as_set` loses weakness markers, meaning even if `include_weak=True` is passed it's impossible to tell what the data actually means unless you call it twice and subtract the sets.
- `__len__`, `__iter__`, and `__contains__` all act on the strong set only. But `__bool__` looks at the star tag and weak set too, which is correct for how this class is actually used. `__len__` and `__iter__` are incorrect, they don't represent how many values are contained in the collection (and can't with star), it's not clear why they would be used. `__contains__` is a less clear version of calling `contains`.
- `contains` should probably be renamed to `contains_strong` to mirror `contains_weak` and make it even clearer what's being used.
- With all that, there's no reason for this to inherit `Collection` at all.

pr.title: tracing: add Instrumented::span_and_inner_pin_mut
pr.body:
This is useful for implementing poll-type functions on foreign traits.

Closes #2804.

There's some potential for bikeshedding about names; I don't care one way or another, and so I used the name that the internal code is already using on the projection type.

Most use cases probably won't need `&mut Span` as opposed to `&Span`, but the mutable reference is actually natural and fully general here: the inner value really does need to be a pinned mutable reference (because that's what's used in poll-type functions), so the `Instrumented` value also needs to be behind a mutable reference, so there's never an opportunity to create a second reference to the span while the reference to the inner value is held.

There's potential for a `span_and_inner_pin_ref` method, which also already exists on the projection type, but I don't know what the use case for exposing that is as opposed to using the existing methods (since mutable references and exclusivity aren't in play).

issue.title: Use the COLUMNS env var to learn the terminal width
issue.body:
Currently, delta queries only the terminal using the TIOCGWINSZ ioctl to know the window width, and falls back to a default of 80 when output is not a tty. This is a problem for hosts running delta in a pipe in order to render its output in a view; they have to jump through hoops to let users include a `--width` argument in the delta command.

Lazygit is such a host: it used to run the git command with delta as a GIT_PAGER in a pty, but we recently had to change this on Windows because our pty implementation there won't work well with the upcoming OSC 1717 feature. We now run git and delta in a pipe without a pty, and setting COLUMNS would allow us to not make this a breaking change for users.

Here's a PR that implements this: #2240. Disclaimer: it was created by Claude, but I reviewed it thoroughly and made the important decisions together with Claude; in particular the one that COLUMNS takes precedence over ioctl. I think this makes sense because git does the same, and because it gives hosts a way to override the terminal width should they have a reason to do that (lazygit doesn't).

pr.title: Take the terminal width from $COLUMNS when it is set
pr.body:
Delta learns how wide to render by asking the terminal on its stdout. A caller that runs delta with no terminal there cannot state a width, so delta falls back to 80 columns. Editors and TUIs that render delta's output into one of their own views hit this, and have to pass --width on every invocation.

Read $COLUMNS first, and ask the terminal only if $COLUMNS is unset or does not hold a positive number. Git resolves the width the same way in term_columns(), and sets $COLUMNS for the pager it spawns, because its own stdout is a pipe to that pager by then and the ioctl no longer reaches a terminal. Following git keeps delta and the git process feeding it on the same width. An explicit --width still wins over both.

Fixes #2239.
